Stem cells made from ordinary adult cells, first reported in 2006 by Shinya Yamanaka and Kazutoshi Takahashi at Kyoto University. They added four genes to skin cells of mice, and the cells went back to an embryo-like state from which they could grow into almost any kind of cell. In 2007 Yamanaka's team, and separately James Thomson's in Wisconsin, did the same with human cells.

Before this, such cells came mainly from human embryos, which raised ethical objections and legal limits in many countries. Induced pluripotent stem cells, or iPS cells, avoid that. Scientists can grow a patient's own cells to study disease and test drugs, and trials have begun of iPS cells for eye disease and Parkinson's.

Yamanaka shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2012 with John Gurdon, who had shown in 1962 that the nucleus of a frog's body cell still held all the instructions for a whole animal. The discovery was a high point of science in modern Japan.
